title: Harmanpreet Kaur Unveils Wax Statue in Jaipur, Says 171 Knock Changed Women's Cricket
excerpt: The former India captain's figure will stand permanently beside Tendulkar and Dhoni at Nahargarh Fort. At the unveiling she credited her 171-run innings with changing perceptions, and told young women cricketers to bat like Vaibhav Sooryavanshi.
body:
• Harmanpreet Kaur's wax statue was unveiled in Jaipur on Friday, placing her alongside Sachin Tendulkar and Mahendra Singh Dhoni at the Historica museum at Nahargarh Fort.
  • Organisers say the figure, crafted by the Historica Museum, is the world's first wax statue of a female cricketer and will be on permanent display.
  • Harmanpreet said her 171-run knock changed how India perceived women's cricket, and compared the women's World Cup triumph's impact to the men's 1983 win.
  • She urged young women cricketers to copy Vaibhav Sooryavanshi's fearless approach: "He has set an example by the way he plays."

Harmanpreet Kaur joined a short list on Friday. Her wax statue was unveiled at a ceremony at the Rajasthan International Centre in Jaipur, putting Indian women's cricket's most recognisable face in the company of Sachin Tendulkar, Mahendra Singh Dhoni and Virat Kohli — the male legends who have long monopolised that form of honour.

The figure was crafted by the Historica Museum, whose organisers noted it is the world's first wax statue of a female cricketer. It will be placed on permanent display at the 'Historica: Step into History' museum at Nahargarh Fort, alongside the statues of Tendulkar and Dhoni. Young aspiring cricketers from Jaipur welcomed her with a guard of honour of raised bats, and Harmanpreet interacted with them and posed for photographs, according to IANS.

"This is just the beginning. Women's cricket will reach even greater heights in the coming years."

— Harmanpreet Kaur

The innings that started it

Reflecting on her career at the unveiling, Harmanpreet said her historic 171-run knock played a pivotal role in transforming public perception of women's cricket in India. She observed that the sport has since undergone a marked shift, with stadiums drawing packed crowds and growing numbers of women turning out to cheer for the national side. Describing the team's maiden Women's ODI World Cup triumph as a dream come true and the result of years of hard work, she drew a parallel with India's 1983 men's World Cup victory, saying the women's success had similarly reshaped the landscape of the game — and expressed confidence the team would keep winning trophies.

She described seeing her statue displayed alongside the cricketers she grew up admiring as a deeply emotional milestone, the product of years of perseverance and early-career struggle, and praised the sculptors for the detailed measurements, photographs and video recordings used to build the likeness.

Her advice to the next generation

Speaking to reporters in Jaipur, Harmanpreet pointed to a 15-year-old as the model for young women cricketers to follow. "Vaibhav Sooryavanshi has set an example by the way he plays," she said, as quoted by ANI. "I'm sure that the new young girls coming up will also play aggressive cricket like this, and across the entire country and the entire world, they will change the image of women's cricket." Sooryavanshi, the Rajasthan Royals opener, made his India debut at 15 and has built a reputation for explosive batting.

Harmanpreet also made the case for grassroots investment, pointing out that India's villages and small towns hold immense sporting potential — she comes from a similar background herself — and calling for greater encouragement and better sporting infrastructure for aspiring female athletes in rural areas. State associations and the BCCI, she added, now run an almost year-round cricketing calendar that gives emerging players a stronger platform for professional careers. Harmanpreet stepped down as India's captain across formats in October but continues to play for the national side.
